entries.name: ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A glowing ball seen during thunderstorms that lasts a few seconds. It seems to appear at random and may vanish with or without a trace.
entries.background: No accepted explanation exists, and it has almost never been recorded by instruments. Most knowledge comes from eyewitness accounts.

entries.name: François Arago
entries.background: French astronomer and physicist of the early 1800s. His 1837 work on thunder gave the phenomenon the name ball lightning.

entries.name: Vladimir Lvovich Bychkov
entries.background: Russian physics professor who has kept a database of ball lightning reports. Several of the Russian cases come from his files.

entries.name: fragmented science
entries.senseHere: The state of ball lightning research, where people collect data, theorize or run lab tests separately without a shared framework.

entries.name: Prairie Meteorite Network
entries.background: A network of cameras in the US Midwest that photographed the night sky daily to track meteors. Its photos were searched for ball lightning.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.background: The Austrian network of sensors that records the time, place and strength of lightning strikes. Its data were compared with ball lightning reports.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.background: The German lightning location network, which records where and when lightning strikes and with what current.

entries.name: positive lightning stroke
entries.background: A lightning flash that carries positive charge to the ground, rarer than the usual negative kind. Such strokes are often much stronger.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: Austrian geologist and mineralogist in Vienna, a member of the Imperial Academy of Sciences. He described the 1868 Vienna fireballs to the Academy.

entries.name: Axel D. Wittmann
entries.background: German astrophysicist at Göttingen. As a child in 1951 he saw a ball that split into smaller balls, and he later worked out their energy from melted asphalt.

entries.name: Othniel Charles Marsh
entries.background: American palaeontologist at Yale, known for discovering many dinosaur fossils. He was president of the US National Academy of Sciences.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: German experimental physicist. With Otto Stern he did the 1922 experiment showing that atomic spin takes only certain discrete orientations in a magnetic field.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: British radio astronomer who later became a professor of physical electronics. His report of a glowing ball drifting down an airliner aisle in 1963 became famous.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: Baltic German physicist in St Petersburg who was electrocuted in 1753 while studying atmospheric electricity. A popular engraving showed a lightning ball striking him.

entries.name: Frankenstein
entries.background: Mary Shelley's 1818 novel about a scientist whose experiment brings a creature to life and ends in disaster.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: French physician, a founder of modern neurology, who taught Sigmund Freud. He examined a patient hit by ball lightning at the Salpêtrière hospital in Paris in 1889.

entries.name: keraunoparalysis
entries.background: Temporary paralysis and numbness after a lightning strike, which usually fades within hours. Charcot separated it from lasting nervous disorders.

entries.name: Sigmund Freud
entries.background: Austrian founder of psychoanalysis. He studied under Charcot in Paris and translated his lectures into German.

entries.name: Dorstone case
entries.background: A 1936 report from Herefordshire, UK, of a red-hot ball that fell into a tub of water and made it boil. Researchers used it to estimate the ball's energy.

entries.name: Poughquag glass
entries.background: A 2008 sighting at a house in Poughquag, New York. The glass of the porch door was later tested for the radiation the ball might have given off.

entries.name: Camp Blanding experiment
entries.background: Experiment at a Florida military base where lightning was triggered by rockets trailing wire and aimed at over 100 ground materials. It produced glowing effects but not true ball lightning.

entries.name: Qinghai spectrum
entries.background: A 2012 video recording on the Qinghai Plateau in China of a ball lightning, captured with spectroscopic cameras. Its light showed lines of iron, silicon, calcium, nitrogen and oxygen.

entries.name: Mitino incident
entries.background: A 2015 sighting in a Moscow district, filmed by three people on mobile phones. Triangulating the videos gave the object's height and speed.
